title: The hidden intricacies of Messier 106
caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 106, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 106, NGC 4258 · constellation Canes Venatici · about 23 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #62 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A small, bright core floods the centre of this galaxy with bluish-white light, while broad swirling streaks of red and orange gas and dust mark its arms and two extra arms show up in green. This is Messier 106, also called NGC 4258, a spiral about 23 million light-years away in Canes Venatici, seen by Webb's NIRCam.

Like most spirals it has a supermassive black hole at its heart, but this one is unusually busy. The Milky Way's black hole only now and then draws in wisps of gas, while M106's is steadily consuming material, which heats up and radiates strongly as it spirals in. Webb observed it to study this active galactic nucleus.

The galaxy is known for two anomalous extra arms, seen in radio and X-rays rather than visible light and made of hot gas rather than stars. Astronomers believe the black hole's activity creates them, much like a wave bursting upward when it strikes a rock near the shore.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.85 x 4.88 arcminutes) and distance (23 million light years), the frame spans roughly 26,000 × 33,000 light-years. Its light set out about 23 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light. Blue shows stars, orange warmer dust, red colder dust, and teal, green and yellow trace gas near the centre.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the extra arms are normally detected in radio and X-rays rather than visible light.

explore: Blue shows the spread of stars, orange warmer dust and deeper red colder dust, while teal, green and yellow near the centre trace gas. Despite the name, Charles Messier never catalogued it. His assistant Pierre Méchain discovered it, and it joined the catalogue only in the 20th century. Two supernovae have been seen in this galaxy.
alt: The central region of a spiral galaxy with a small bright bluish-white core, red and orange swirling arms of gas and dust, and two extra arms in green.
